hypotheses.title: update_market loop over epochs can be griefed to block sync_ledger and claim
hypotheses.description: `update_market` iterates `while (i < block.number)` in BLOCK_EPOCH (100k block) steps, calling `gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write` each iteration. If a market is left un-updated for many epochs (e.g. low activity), the loop grows unbounded and eventually exceeds the block gas limit, reverting. Since `sync_ledger` and `claim` both call `update_market`, all deposits/withdrawals/claims for that market become permanently uncallable.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or simply natural inactivity) causes a whitelisted market's `lastRewardBlock` to lag far behind `block.number`. 2) Any call to `sync_ledger`/`claim` triggers `update_market`, whose loop over 100k-block epochs plus external `gauge_relative_weight_write` calls (each doing up to 500-iteration loops) exceeds gas. 3) All user operations on that market revert; funds locked in the market cannot be withdrawn via the ledger path.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds and permanently stuck user balances in the lending market; rewards unclaimable; market effectively bricked.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap iterations per call (e.g. process at most N epochs and store progress), or use a bounded catch-up mechanism so `update_market` cannot exceed gas limits.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger update_market uses stale marketSupply for whole loop
hypotheses.description: `update_market` reads `marketSupply = lendingMarketTotalBalance[_market]` once before the while loop and uses it as the divisor for every epoch's `accCantoPerShare` and `secRewardsPerShare` accrual. If the market balance changes between epochs (deposits/withdrawals via `sync_ledger`), the historical accrual is computed against the current balance rather than the balance that actually existed during each epoch, so rewards per share are mispriced. Because `sync_ledger` calls `update_market` before mutating the balance, the balance used is the one at the time of the last sync, not the per-epoch balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a tiny amount into a whitelisted market so `lendingMarketTotalBalance` is small. 2) Attacker waits many epochs without calling `sync_ledger`/`update_market` so `lastRewardBlock` is far behind. 3) Attacker (or anyone) triggers `update_market`; the entire multi-epoch reward is divided by the tiny current supply, inflating `accCantoPerShare` massively. 4) Attacker claims the inflated rewards via `claim`, draining CANTO that should have been distributed across the larger historical supply.
hypotheses.impact: Over-distribution of CANTO rewards to a single late actor; protocol reward pool drained; other lenders' accrued rewards become unclaimable (insolvency of the reward ledger).
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `marketSupply` inside the loop per epoch (or checkpoint on every balance change) so each epoch's accrual uses the balance that existed during that epoch.

hypotheses.title: GaugeController.vote_for_gauge_weights uses stale user slope from last checkpoint
hypotheses.description: The function reads the user's slope via `ve.getLastUserPoint(msg.sender)` which returns the slope recorded at the last checkpoint, not the current slope. Since VotingEscrow slope decays linearly over time, the returned slope is stale and overstates the user's actual current voting power. An attacker can lock tokens, wait for slope decay, and still vote with the original (higher) slope, then repeat to inflate voting power beyond what they actually hold.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `createLock` with a large amount, recording a high slope. 2) Attacker waits for time to pass so the actual bias/slope decays. 3) Attacker calls `vote_for_gauge_weights` — the contract reads the stale slope from `getLastUserPoint` (which is the slope at last checkpoint, not decayed). 4) Attacker votes with inflated weight, then can re-vote repeatedly to shift gauge weights disproportionately.
hypotheses.impact: Gauge weight manipulation — attacker directs disproportionate CANTO emissions to a gauge they control, draining rewards from honest LPs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the current slope by decaying the stored slope by elapsed time (or call `balanceOf` and derive slope from current bias), rather than using the raw stored slope.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.claim() sends CANTO before updating rewardDebt
hypotheses.description: In claim(), the contract computes cantoToSend, then sets user.rewardDebt = accumulatedCanto, and only afterwards performs the external call `msg.sender.call{value: cantoToSend}("")`. Because the recipient is an arbitrary address and the function lacks a reentrancy guard, a malicious contract can re-enter claim() during the callback. On re-entry, user.rewardDebt has already been updated, so the second call computes cantoToSend = 0 and sends nothing — but the attacker can also re-enter sync_ledger() or other functions to manipulate user.amount and market state mid-callback.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that is whitelisted as a lending market (or uses an existing whitelisted market they control) and accrues rewards. 2) Attacker calls claim() from a contract whose receive()/fallback re-enters sync_ledger() to inflate user.amount, or re-enters claim() after manipulating market.accCantoPerShare via update_market(). 3) The reentrant call reads the already-updated rewardDebt but a freshly inflated user.amount, allowing a second payout or double-counting.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claiming of CANTO rewards, draining the contract's CANTO balance and causing insolvency for other lenders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a nonReentrant modifier to claim() and sync_ledger(), and follow checks-effects-interactions by updating all state before the external call.

hypotheses.title: Double-counting of delegated voting power in increaseAmount
hypotheses.description: When a user has delegated their lock to a delegatee (delegatee != msg.sender), increaseAmount() first updates the sender's own lock and checkpoints it, then updates the delegatee's lock by adding the same `_value` to `newLocked.delegated`. However, the sender's own `locked[msg.sender].delegated` was already incremented in the first branch (newLocked.delegated += _value happens before the if/else). This means the same deposited CANTO contributes voting power to both the sender's own lock AND the delegatee's lock, inflating total voting power and gauge weight beyond the actual deposited amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a lock and delegates to a colluding delegatee. 2) Attacker calls increaseAmount() with value V. 3) The sender's lock.delegated increases by V (via newLocked.delegated += _value before the branch), and the delegatee's lock.delegated also increases by V. 4) Both locks now report voting power derived from the same V, doubling the effective weight. 5) Attacker votes with both accounts in GaugeController to capture disproportionate gauge weight and thus disproportionate CANTO rewards from LendingLedger.
hypotheses.impact: Inflated voting power, unfair gauge weight distribution, over-claiming of CANTO rewards from LendingLedger, protocol insolvency of reward pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: In the delegated branch, do not add `_value` to the sender's `newLocked.delegated`; only add it to the delegatee's lock. Restructure so the sender's delegated amount is only incremented when delegatee == msg.sender.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.sync_ledger trusts caller-supplied delta without market validation
hypotheses.description: sync_ledger() accepts an arbitrary int256 _delta from msg.sender and only checks that the market is whitelisted. Any whitelisted market (or an attacker who gets a market whitelisted, or a compromised/upgradeable market) can call sync_ledger with an arbitrary positive delta for any _lender, inflating user.amount and lendingMarketTotalBalance without any actual deposit. There is no verification that the delta corresponds to a real token transfer or that msg.sender is the market for _lender.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls or compromises a whitelisted lending market. 2) Calls sync_ledger(victimOrAttacker, hugePositiveDelta) to inflate user.amount and market balance. 3) Calls claim() to withdraw CANTO rewards proportional to the inflated amount, or manipulates gauge_relative_weight_write() inputs via the inflated market balance.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of CANTO rewards from the LendingLedger, incorrect reward accounting, and potential insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict sync_ledger to trusted market contracts and validate the delta against actual token movements, or require the market to be the caller and the lender to be a known depositor.

hypotheses.title: secRewardsPerShare accrues without any reward token backing
hypotheses.description: `market.secRewardsPerShare += uint128((blockDelta * 1e18) / marketSupply);` accrues secondary rewards per share purely as a function of blockDelta and marketSupply, with no corresponding funding source, no cap, and no token transfer. Any user who deposits into a whitelisted market accrues `secRewardDebt` that grows unboundedly. There is no claim path for secondary rewards in this contract, but the accounting is still wrong and any future claim implementation (or off-chain accounting) would be insolvent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits a tiny amount into a whitelisted market early. 2) Over time, secRewardsPerShare grows linearly with blocks. 3) Attacker's secRewardDebt becomes enormous relative to any real backing. 4) If/when a secondary reward claim is added or off-chain distribution uses this value, attacker drains the entire secondary reward pool.
hypotheses.impact: Unbacked reward accounting, potential total loss of secondary reward funds, protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the secRewardsPerShare accrual or gate it behind an actual funded reward rate with a per-epoch budget, mirroring cantoPerBlock.

hypotheses.title: sync_ledger callable by anyone, spoofing lending market balances
hypotheses.description: sync_ledger() uses msg.sender as the lending market and only checks that it is whitelisted via update_market(). Any external caller can invoke sync_ledger() directly with an arbitrary _lender and _delta, since there is no check that msg.sender is actually a whitelisted lending market performing a legitimate deposit/withdrawal. The function then mutates userInfo and lendingMarketTotalBalance for msg.sender's market.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a whitelisted lending market address M. 2) Attacker calls M.sync_ledger(attacker, hugePositiveDelta) — but msg.sender is the attacker, not M, so this fails. Wait: msg.sender must be M. However, if any whitelisted market exposes a public function that forwards to sync_ledger, or if the attacker can call sync_ledger from a contract they control that is whitelisted... Actually the real issue: sync_ledger trusts msg.sender == market, but there is no authentication that the caller is the market contract itself beyond whitelist. If the market address is an EOA or a contract with a public passthrough, attacker can inflate user.amount and rewardDebt, then claim() drains CANTO.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can inflate their user.amount and rewardDebt in a whitelisted market, then call claim() to drain CANTO rewards from the contract, causing loss of funds and incorrect accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require that msg.sender is the actual lending market contract (e.g., verify via a registry or callback pattern) and/or restrict sync_ledger to a known market interface; do not rely solely on whitelist membership of msg.sender.

hypotheses.title: GaugeController.vote_for_gauge_weights allows voting with expired lock
hypotheses.description: The function reads `slope_` from `ve.getLastUserPoint(msg.sender)` and requires `slope_ >= 0`, but does not verify that the user's lock is still active beyond `lock_end > next_time`. If a user's lock has expired (`lock_end <= block.timestamp`), `getLastUserPoint` returns the last recorded point whose `slope` may still be positive (the slope is only zeroed at checkpoint time). The check `lock_end > next_time` prevents voting after expiry, but a user whose lock expires exactly at `next_time` can still vote because `lock_end > next_time` is false only when `lock_end <= next_time`. More critically, `slope` is taken from the last user point without recomputing the current bias, so a user whose voting power has decayed to zero can still cast a vote with the stale slope.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user locks tokens, waits until their voting power has decayed to near zero (but before `lock_end`), then calls `vote_for_gauge_weights` with `_user_weight = 10_000`. The stale `slope` from `getLastUserPoint` is used to compute `new_slope.slope`, inflating the gauge weight beyond the user's actual current voting power.
hypotheses.impact: Gauge weights are inflated, causing incorrect CANTO distribution in `LendingLedger.update_market` and potentially draining rewards to the wrong gauges.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `ve.balanceOf(msg.sender)` to derive the current voting power, or call `ve.checkpoint()` before reading the slope.

hypotheses.title: secRewardsPerShare accrues per-block with no reward rate
hypotheses.description: `market.secRewardsPerShare += uint128((blockDelta * 1e18) / marketSupply);` accrues 1e18 per block per unit of supply regardless of any configured secondary reward rate, and the TODO comment confirms the scaling is unfinished. This makes `secRewardDebt` grow unboundedly and inconsistently with any real secondary token accounting, and the value is never used to pay anything, so it silently corrupts user accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any user interacting with a whitelisted market causes `secRewardDebt` to accumulate arbitrary values; if a future claim path is added or if `secRewardDebt` is used in any downstream logic, the inflated debt will misprice claims. Even without a claim path, the stored debt is wrong and can be used to grief accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect user accounting; potential future over-claim of secondary rewards; storage values diverge from real holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the placeholder accrual or gate it behind a real, governance-set secondary reward rate with correct scaling.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.update_market uses gauge_relative_weight_write with past epoch, allowing weight manipulation
hypotheses.description: `update_market` calls `gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write(_market, epoch)` for each past epoch. This function writes/checkpoints gauge weights for the given time. Because `_get_weight` and `_get_sum` iterate forward from the last checkpointed time, calling this with an old epoch can retroactively fill in weights. An attacker who can trigger `update_market` (anyone via `sync_ledger` on a whitelisted market) can cause the gauge weight used for reward calculation to be computed at a time when the attacker had inflated voting power, capturing more rewards than deserved.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker votes heavily on a gauge, then lets the vote expire/decay. 2) Attacker calls `sync_ledger` (or triggers `update_market`) which iterates over past epochs and calls `gauge_relative_weight_write` for each. 3) The write function fills in weights based on the state at those past times, potentially using the attacker's inflated historical weight. 4) Rewards are distributed based on manipulated weights.
hypotheses.impact: Reward misallocation — attacker captures more CANTO rewards than their fair share, draining the reward pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the read-only `gauge_relative_weight` for historical epochs, or ensure weights are checkpointed at the time of the epoch rather than retroactively written.

hypotheses.title: GaugeController vote_for_gauge_weights can be griefed via _get_sum/_get_weight loops
hypotheses.description: `vote_for_gauge_weights` calls `_get_weight` and `_get_sum`, each looping up to 500 iterations of weekly steps. If a gauge or the global sum has not been checkpointed for a long time, these loops run to their maximum, and combined with the rest of the function can exceed the block gas limit, reverting every vote. An attacker can also spam `checkpoint_gauge`/`checkpoint` to keep state fresh, but the reverse (letting it lag) is trivially achievable by inactivity, and any single user's vote can be blocked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits (or induces) a long period without checkpoints on a gauge. 2) When a victim calls `vote_for_gauge_weights`, `_get_weight` and `_get_sum` iterate up to 500 weeks each, consuming excessive gas. 3) The transaction reverts, preventing the victim from voting or changing weights.
hypotheses.impact: Voting functionality can be temporarily or permanently blocked for users; governance weight distribution frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bound the catch-up loops or split checkpointing into separate permissionless calls with progress tracking so voting cannot be gas-griefed.

hypotheses.title: withdraw() reverts on failed native transfer, trapping user funds
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` sends CANTO via `msg.sender.call{value: amountToSend}("")` and requires success. If the recipient is a contract that reverts on receive (or consumes more than the 2300 gas stipend in a fallback), the entire withdrawal reverts. Because the lock state is updated before the call but the whole tx reverts, the user cannot withdraw at all, and there is no alternative recipient parameter or recovery path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A user's lock is held by a contract (e.g. a smart contract wallet or vault) whose `receive`/`fallback` reverts or is gas-heavy. 2) Calling `withdraw` reverts on the transfer. 3) The user has no way to specify an alternate recipient, so the locked CANTO is permanently stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Locked CANTO permanently frozen for affected users; no recovery mechanism.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow specifying a recipient address for the withdrawal, or use a pull-based claim pattern so a reverting receiver cannot block the state transition.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.sync_ledger trusts msg.sender as market without signature
hypotheses.description: `sync_ledger` uses `msg.sender` as the lending market and only checks `lendingMarketWhitelist[msg.sender]` inside `update_market`. Any whitelisted market can call `sync_ledger` for arbitrary `_lender` addresses and arbitrary `_delta` values, including negative deltas that reduce another user's `amount` and `rewardDebt`. There is no signature or authorization from the lender. A malicious or compromised whitelisted market can grief users by zeroing their balances or inflating them.
hypotheses.attackPath: A whitelisted market (attacker-controlled or compromised) calls `sync_ledger(victim, -victimBalance)` to zero the victim's `user.amount` and `rewardDebt`, or calls with a large positive delta to inflate `lendingMarketTotalBalance` and dilute other users' rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Theft/griefing of user rewards; incorrect `lendingMarketTotalBalance` leading to reward dilution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the lender to authorize the delta (e.g., via signature or by having the market be the lender's own contract), or restrict `sync_ledger` to be called only by the lender themselves.

hypotheses.title: update_market loop can be griefed to run out of gas / skip rewards
hypotheses.description: The while loop iterates from `market.lastRewardBlock` to `block.number` in BLOCK_EPOCH chunks. If a market is whitelisted and then not touched for a very long time (many epochs), the loop can exceed the block gas limit, causing update_market (and thus sync_ledger and claim) to revert permanently. Since sync_ledger is called by the market on every deposit/withdraw, this bricks the market's ledger integration.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or simply inactivity) causes a whitelisted market to go untouched for a large number of blocks. 2) Any subsequent call to sync_ledger or claim reverts due to gas. 3) Users cannot deposit, withdraw, or claim; funds effectively frozen in the ledger accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on reward accounting, frozen user rewards, inability to sync deposits/withdrawals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the number of iterations per call and allow resuming from the last processed block, or use a pull-based per-epoch checkpoint pattern.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.update_market uses wrong epoch for cantoPerBlock lookup
hypotheses.description: The loop computes `epoch = (i / BLOCK_EPOCH) * BLOCK_EPOCH` and then reads `cantoPerBlock[epoch]`, but `setRewards` stores rewards keyed by the epoch start block. When `i` is exactly at an epoch boundary the value is correct, but the loop advances `i += blockDelta` where `blockDelta = min(nextEpoch, block.number) - i`, so `i` lands exactly on `nextEpoch` (a multiple of BLOCK_EPOCH) and the next iteration reads the correct epoch. However, `nextEpoch = i + BLOCK_EPOCH` is computed from the current `i`, not from the epoch boundary, so if `i` is not aligned (e.g. after a partial first iteration), `nextEpoch` is not a multiple of BLOCK_EPOCH and the subsequent `epoch` lookup is misaligned, causing rewards to be read from the wrong epoch bucket.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker (any user) can call `sync_ledger` on a whitelisted market at a block number that is not aligned to BLOCK_EPOCH, forcing `update_market` to iterate with a misaligned `i`. The misaligned `nextEpoch` causes `epoch` to be computed from a non-boundary `i`, reading `cantoPerBlock` for the wrong epoch (often 0), which either under-credits or over-credits `accCantoPerShare`.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward accounting; users can claim more or fewer CANTO than entitled, potentially draining the contract's CANTO balance or leaving rewards stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `nextEpoch = ((i / BLOCK_EPOCH) + 1) * BLOCK_EPOCH` so the boundary is always aligned to BLOCK_EPOCH.

hypotheses.title: claim() can be called by anyone for any market, draining rewards
hypotheses.description: claim(address _market) is external and has no access control. It calls update_market(_market) which only checks whitelist, then reads userInfo[_market][msg.sender] and sends CANTO to msg.sender. Any user can call claim() for any whitelisted market, but the reward is computed from their own userInfo. The real issue is that userInfo can be manipulated via sync_ledger (see above) or that claim() does not verify the caller has a legitimate position. Combined with sync_ledger being callable, an attacker can inflate their user.amount and rewardDebt and then claim.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of CANTO funds from the LendingLedger contract; attacker can drain rewards without providing any cNOTE.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure sync_ledger is properly authenticated so userInfo cannot be inflated; consider adding a check that the caller is the market or that user.amount reflects real deposits.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.update_market loop can be griefed via unbounded iterations
hypotheses.description: The `while (i < block.number)` loop iterates over every BLOCK_EPOCH (100,000 blocks) between `market.lastRewardBlock` and current block. If a market is whitelisted and then not updated for a long time, the loop can run many iterations, potentially exceeding block gas limits. An attacker can prevent `update_market` from succeeding by simply not calling it (or by making the market inactive), causing `sync_ledger` and `claim` to revert for all users of that market.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until a whitelisted market has not been updated for a very long time (many epochs). 2) Attacker calls `sync_ledger` or `claim` on that market. 3) The `update_market` loop runs out of gas, reverting the transaction. 4) All users of that market are unable to sync or claim rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service — users cannot claim rewards or update their positions in the affected market.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the number of iterations per call, or allow partial updates with a resumable cursor.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.withdraw() external call after state update but no reentrancy on checkpoint
hypotheses.description: withdraw() updates locked[msg.sender] and calls _checkpoint() before sending CANTO via `msg.sender.call{value: amountToSend}("")`. Although nonReentrant is present, the external call happens after state updates, which is correct ordering. However, the recipient can re-enter other contracts (e.g., GaugeController.vote_for_gauge_weights) that read VotingEscrow state mid-transaction, and the checkpoint's slopeChanges updates may not yet reflect the withdrawal in dependent contracts. More critically, the receive() callback can call GaugeController functions that read getLastUserPoint() and lockEnd() while the withdrawal is still in flight, potentially causing inconsistent vote weight accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker with an expired lock calls withdraw(). 2) In the receive() callback, attacker calls GaugeController.vote_for_gauge_weights() or checkpoint_gauge() which reads VotingEscrow state. 3) Because the withdrawal's checkpoint has already zeroed the user's delegated amount but the CANTO has not yet been received, the attacker can vote with stale or manipulated weights.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect gauge weight accounting, potential manipulation of reward distribution in LendingLedger via gauge_relative_weight_write().
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure dependent contracts (GaugeController) cannot be called during the withdrawal callback, or move the external call to the very end after all cross-contract state is consistent.

hypotheses.title: remove_gauge_weight loop over 263 weeks can revert on large slope changes
hypotheses.description: `_remove_gauge_weight` loops 263 times subtracting `changes_sum[time_to_check] -= gauge_weight_change`. If `changes_sum[time_to_check]` is smaller than `gauge_weight_change` (possible due to prior manual slope cancellations or overlapping gauge removals), the subtraction underflows and reverts. Since `remove_gauge` and `remove_gauge_weight` are the only paths to disable a gauge, a reverting removal leaves the gauge permanently active and its weight stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or normal operation) creates overlapping slope changes across gauges such that `changes_sum[t]` is less than a gauge's recorded `changes_weight[t]`. 2) Governance attempts `remove_gauge`/`remove_gauge_weight`; the loop underflows and reverts. 3) The gauge cannot be removed, and its weight continues to consume the sum, distorting all relative weights.
hypotheses.impact: Gauge cannot be removed; global weight accounting corrupted; rewards misallocated; potential permanent stuck state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use saturating subtraction (e.g. `changes_sum[t] = changes_sum[t] > gauge_weight_change ? changes_sum[t] - gauge_weight_change : 0`) as already done in `vote_for_gauge_weights`.

hypotheses.title: claim() reverts on failed native transfer, blocking reward claims
hypotheses.description: `claim` sends CANTO via `msg.sender.call{value: cantoToSend}("")` and requires success. If the caller is a contract that reverts on receive, the claim reverts. Although `user.rewardDebt` is updated before the call, the revert rolls it back, so the user can never claim. There is no alternate recipient or pull mechanism.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A contract-based user (e.g. multisig, vault) with a reverting or gas-heavy receive calls `claim`. 2) The transfer reverts, rolling back `rewardDebt`. 3) Rewards remain permanently unclaimable for that address.
hypotheses.impact: Accrued CANTO rewards permanently stuck for affected users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Support a recipient parameter or use a pull-based withdrawal pattern so a reverting receiver cannot block claims.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.claim lacks reentrancy guard allowing reward double-claim
hypotheses.description: `claim()` sends CANTO via a raw `call` to `msg.sender` before the function returns, and the contract has no `nonReentrant` modifier. Although `user.rewardDebt` is updated before the external call, the attacker can re-enter `claim()` (or `sync_ledger`) during the callback. Because `update_market` is idempotent within the same block (lastRewardBlock == block.number), re-entering `claim` will compute `cantoToSend = accumulatedCanto - user.rewardDebt` which is now 0, so direct double-claim of the same debt is blocked — but re-entering `sync_ledger` with a positive delta from a malicious whitelisted market can inflate `user.amount` and `rewardDebt` inconsistently, and re-entering `claim` after manipulating state via a malicious market callback can drain funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys/controls a whitelisted lending market (or exploits a market that calls back). 2) Attacker calls `claim()`; during the CANTO `call` callback, the attacker's contract re-enters `sync_ledger` with a crafted `_delta` to alter `user.amount`/`rewardDebt`, then calls `claim()` again to extract additional CANTO before the outer call's state settles. 3) Repeat to drain the contract's CANTO balance.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of CANTO rewards held by LendingLedger; accounting corruption of `userInfo` and `lendingMarketTotalBalance`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `claim()` and `sync_ledger()`, and use `ReentrancyGuard` from OpenZeppelin.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.increaseAmount delegatee path can be griefed via delegatee lock expiry
hypotheses.description: In the delegated branch of `increaseAmount`, after updating the sender's lock, the code reads `locked[delegatee]` and requires `locked_.amount > 0` and `locked_.end > block.timestamp`. If the delegatee's lock has expired or been withdrawn, the entire transaction reverts, even though the sender's own lock update was already written to storage in the same transaction (it will be rolled back). This means a sender whose delegatee has withdrawn cannot increase their own lock until they undelegate, which is a griefing vector if the delegatee intentionally withdraws to block the sender.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (delegatee) waits until a victim has delegated to them, then calls `withdraw()` to zero their lock. The victim's subsequent `increaseAmount` calls revert, locking the victim out of increasing their lock until they call `undelegate` (if such a function exists — it does not appear in this file, so the victim may be permanently stuck).
hypotheses.impact: Victim's funds are locked; they cannot increase their lock or earn additional voting power. If no undelegate function exists, the victim may be unable to withdraw their delegated amount.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow the sender to update their own lock even if the delegatee's lock is invalid, or provide an `undelegate` function that lets the sender reclaim their delegated amount.

hypotheses.title: claim() can be front-run by deposit to dilute or by withdraw to escape debt
hypotheses.description: `claim()` calls `update_market` which accrues rewards up to the current block, then computes `cantoToSend = accumulatedCanto - user.rewardDebt`. A user can deposit right before a large reward accrual (or right before another user's claim triggers update_market) to capture a share of rewards for blocks during which they held no balance, because `sync_ledger` credits `rewardDebt` using the current `accCantoPerShare` which already includes the just-accrued rewards. Conversely, a user can withdraw just before an update to avoid negative debt adjustments.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes pending rewards accruing in a market. 2) Attacker deposits a large amount just before any update_market call. 3) update_market accrues rewards for the whole elapsed period, and attacker's sync_ledger credits them with a share of those past rewards via rewardDebt. 4) Attacker claims and withdraws, capturing rewards for time they were not present.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair reward distribution, dilution of honest LPs' rewards, value extraction from the reward pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Accrue rewards before applying the deposit (call update_market first, which is done, but the issue is that the deposit itself is credited at the post-accrual share; instead, snapshot the user's share at the moment of deposit and only accrue future rewards to them). Ensure rewardDebt is set based on accCantoPerShare at deposit time and that no retroactive rewards are credited.

hypotheses.title: LendingLedger.claim lacks reentrancy protection on CANTO transfer
hypotheses.description: `claim` updates `user.rewardDebt = accumulatedCanto` before sending CANTO via `msg.sender.call{value: cantoToSend}("")`. Although `rewardDebt` is updated first, `update_market` is called at the start and `user.amount` is not zeroed, so a reentrant call to `claim` (or `sync_ledger`) during the callback can re-read the same `accCantoPerShare` and `user.amount` and compute a fresh `cantoToSend` because `rewardDebt` was already set to `accumulatedCanto` — but if the attacker re-enters `sync_ledger` with a positive delta, `user.amount` increases and `rewardDebt` increases proportionally, allowing a second claim of the newly accrued rewards in the same transaction.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a contract that calls `claim(market)`. In the `receive()` fallback, it calls `sync_ledger(attacker, delta)` to inflate `user.amount` and `rewardDebt`, then calls `claim(market)` again. Because `update_market` sees `block.number == market.lastRewardBlock` it does not accrue new rewards, but the inflated `user.amount` combined with the already-updated `rewardDebt` can yield a positive `cantoToSend` if `accCantoPerShare` was not fully accounted.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claiming of CANTO rewards, draining the contract's CANTO balance and leaving other users unable to claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `claim` and `sync_ledger`, or use a pull-pattern with a separate withdrawal function.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.increaseAmount resets lock end but not delegated amount for delegatee
hypotheses.description: When a user has delegated their lock to a delegatee, `increaseAmount` updates the sender's lock (`newLocked.end = _floorToWeek(block.timestamp + LOCKTIME)`) and then updates the delegatee's lock by adding `_value` to `newLocked.delegated`. However, the delegatee's `newLocked.end` is not extended — it remains the delegatee's original lock end. This means the delegatee's voting power is computed with the delegatee's old end time, while the sender's lock end is extended. The sender's `delegated` amount is also not increased (only `amount` is), so the sender's own voting power is reduced relative to their locked amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user delegates to a delegatee, then calls `increaseAmount` with a large `_value`. The delegatee's voting power is increased by `_value` but with the delegatee's old end time, while the sender's lock end is extended. The sender can then call `withdraw` after their lock expires (which is later than the delegatee's), but the delegatee's voting power was already inflated.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent voting power accounting between sender and delegatee; the delegatee may have more voting power than the sender's locked amount justifies, and the sender may be unable to withdraw because their `delegated` amount was not increased.
hypotheses.recommendation: When increasing amount on a delegated lock, also extend the delegatee's lock end and update the sender's `delegated` amount consistently.

hypotheses.title: update_market() callable by anyone, allowing reward manipulation
hypotheses.description: update_market(address _market) is public and only requires the market to be whitelisted. Any external caller can trigger reward accrual for any whitelisted market at any time. While this is intended to be permissionless, it interacts with gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write() which can be manipulated. More importantly, an attacker can call update_market() repeatedly to force reward accrual at specific block numbers, potentially front-running or manipulating accCantoPerShare.
hypotheses.impact: An attacker can manipulate the timing of reward accrual, potentially causing incorrect reward distribution or griefing other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Consider whether update_market should be restricted or whether the reward accrual logic is robust against arbitrary callers.

hypotheses.title: checkpoint() and checkpoint_gauge() callable by anyone, allowing state manipulation
hypotheses.description: checkpoint() and checkpoint_gauge() are external and permissionless. They call _get_sum() and _get_weight() which mutate state (points_sum, points_weight, time_sum, time_weight). While intended to be permissionless, an attacker can call these functions to force state updates at specific times, potentially manipulating the timing of weight changes.
hypotheses.impact: Minor manipulation of gauge weight state; unlikely to cause direct loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: This is likely intended behavior; no change needed unless specific manipulation vectors are identified.

hypotheses.title: increaseAmount allows delegation to a delegatee with expired lock
hypotheses.description: In increaseAmount(), when the sender has delegated to a delegatee, the code checks that the delegatee's lock is active (locked_.amount > 0 && locked_.end > block.timestamp). However, if the delegatee's lock expires between the sender's checkpoint and the delegatee's checkpoint, the require will revert. More importantly, the function allows the sender to increase their delegated amount even if the delegatee's lock is about to expire, potentially causing the delegatee's voting power to be inflated incorrectly.
hypotheses.impact: Potential for incorrect voting power accounting for the delegatee.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure delegatee's lock is sufficiently long or handle expiration gracefully.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow balanceOfAt blockTime estimation can underflow bias
hypotheses.description: `blockTime` is estimated from `point0.ts + (dTime * (_blockNumber - point0.blk)) / dBlock`. If `_blockNumber < point0.blk` (possible when the binary search returns an epoch whose blk is greater than the requested block due to the initial point), the subtraction underflows and reverts, or if `blockTime < upoint.ts` the subsequent `blockTime - upoint.ts` underflows. This makes historical balance queries revert for certain block ranges.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any external caller querying `balanceOfAt` for a block number that falls between the initial point and the first user point can trigger a revert, breaking integrations that rely on historical balances (e.g., snapshot voting).
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on historical balance queries; integrations relying on `balanceOfAt` fail.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against `_blockNumber < point0.blk` and clamp `blockTime` to be at least `upoint.ts`.

hypotheses.title: GaugeController._get_sum and _get_weight can be griefed with 500-iteration loops
hypotheses.description: `_get_sum` and `_get_weight` loop up to 500 times to fill in missed weekly checkpoints. If a gauge or the global sum has not been checkpointed for a long time (e.g., 500+ weeks), the loop will not complete the fill, leaving stale data. More critically, if the loop runs out of gas, any function calling it (including `vote_for_gauge_weights`, `gauge_relative_weight_write`) will revert. An attacker can avoid checkpointing for a long period, then trigger a call that reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker ensures no one calls `checkpoint` or `checkpoint_gauge` for a long period (or the contract is simply inactive). 2) Attacker calls `vote_for_gauge_weights` or `gauge_relative_weight_write`. 3) The internal loop runs 500 iterations and may run out of gas, reverting. 4) Voting and weight queries are blocked.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service — gauge voting and weight queries are blocked until someone can afford the gas.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reduce the loop bound or allow partial checkpointing with a resumable state.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.balanceOfAt uses block number estimation that can be manipulated
hypotheses.description: `balanceOfAt` estimates the timestamp of a past block using the average block time between two checkpoints (`dTime * (_blockNumber - point0.blk) / dBlock`). This estimation is inaccurate if block times vary, and can be manipulated by an attacker who controls block production timing (e.g., via validator collusion or by timing transactions around checkpoints). The resulting bias calculation can be wrong, giving incorrect historical voting power.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker times their lock creation/checkpoint to coincide with a period of unusual block times. 2) Attacker queries `balanceOfAt` for a block in that period. 3) The estimated block time is off, causing the bias calculation to be wrong. 4) Attacker uses the incorrect balance for governance or reward calculations.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect historical voting power — could be used to manipulate governance outcomes or reward calculations that rely on `balanceOfAt`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store block timestamps directly in checkpoints, or use a more robust block time oracle.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.increaseAmount updates delegatee lock without reentrancy guard on cross-contract reads
hypotheses.description: increaseAmount() updates the sender's lock, then reads and updates the delegatee's lock, calling _checkpoint() twice. If the delegatee is a contract that can observe state mid-transaction (e.g., via a token callback or a view called from another contract), it can read inconsistent state between the two checkpoints. Since CANTO is native and no callback occurs here, the risk is limited to cross-contract reads during the same transaction from other protocols.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sets a malicious contract as delegatee. 2) Attacker calls increaseAmount(). 3) During the second _checkpoint() (delegatee update), the malicious delegatee's fallback is not triggered (native transfer), but a separate contract called in the same transaction can read the partially-updated state.
hypotheses.impact: Minor accounting inconsistencies in dependent protocols reading VotingEscrow mid-transaction.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document that VotingEscrow state is not safe to read mid-transaction, or add a reentrancy guard that also blocks cross-contract reads via a transient storage flag.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.withdraw lacks reentrancy guard on native CANTO send
hypotheses.description: `withdraw()` is marked `nonReentrant`, but the state update order combined with the raw `call` to `msg.sender` means a malicious contract can re-enter other functions. Specifically, `locked[msg.sender]` is set to a zeroed lock before the call, so re-entering `withdraw()` reverts on `locked_.amount > 0`. However, re-entering `createLock()` or `increaseAmount()` during the callback is possible because those functions are also `nonReentrant` — the guard blocks them. The real issue is that `_checkpoint` is called with `newLocked.delegated = 0` after `locked[msg.sender]` was already written, and the `call` uses all remaining gas; if the recipient is a contract that reverts, funds are stuck. More critically, the `nonReentrant` guard is present, so this is a lower-severity concern.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker with an expired lock calls `withdraw()`; if the guard were absent, they could re-enter `createLock` to re-lock and re-withdraw. With the guard present, this is mitigated.
hypotheses.impact: Potential double-withdraw if guard were removed; currently mitigated.
hypotheses.recommendation: Keep `nonReentrant`; consider `call` with limited gas or pull-payment pattern.

hypotheses.title: GaugeController.vote_for_gauge_weights missing nonce/deadline allows replay of votes
hypotheses.description: `vote_for_gauge_weights` is called directly by `msg.sender` (no signature), so there is no signature replay issue here. However, the function does not enforce a minimum time between votes or a deadline, and `last_user_vote` is recorded but never checked. A user can call this function repeatedly in the same block to manipulate `points_weight`/`points_sum` and `changes_weight`/`changes_sum` in ways that may not be idempotent, potentially causing accounting drift. This is a state-consistency issue rather than a signature replay.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `vote_for_gauge_weights` multiple times in one block with different weights; each call recomputes `old_slope` from `vote_user_slopes` and adjusts `points_weight`/`points_sum` accordingly. If the math is not perfectly reversible, the attacker can inflate their effective weight.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect gauge weight accounting; potential misallocation of CANTO rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `last_user_vote[msg.sender][_gauge_addr] < block.timestamp` or a cooldown, and verify the update math is exactly reversible.

hypotheses.title: GaugeController._remove_gauge_weight loop bound may miss slope changes
hypotheses.description: `_remove_gauge_weight` iterates `i` from 0 to 262 (263 iterations) checking `changes_weight[_gauge][next_time + i * WEEK]`. If a gauge's slope change was scheduled beyond 263 weeks (about 5 years), it will not be cancelled, leaving stale `changes_sum` entries that can later be applied incorrectly. Given the 5-year lock time in VotingEscrow, this is borderline but possible.
hypotheses.attackPath: Governance adds a gauge, users vote with long lock ends, then governance removes the gauge. If any slope change was scheduled beyond 263 weeks, it remains in `changes_sum` and will be applied when `_get_sum` iterates, corrupting total weight.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect total weight accounting; misallocation of rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Increase the loop bound to cover the maximum lock duration (e.g., 5 years / WEEK + buffer) or track scheduled changes per gauge in a list.

hypotheses.title: setRewards can overwrite past epochs and retroactively change rewards
hypotheses.description: `setRewards` allows governance to set `cantoPerBlock[epoch]` for any epoch including past ones, with no restriction that `_fromEpoch` be in the future. Since `update_market` reads `cantoPerBlock[epoch]` lazily during accrual, a past epoch's reward rate can be changed after the fact, retroactively altering rewards for users who already accrued or claimed. While governance is trusted, the code also allows setting rewards for epochs that have already been partially processed, creating inconsistency between already-claimed and future-claimed amounts.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but any user who claims early vs. late gets different amounts for the same epoch, and a governance change can retroactively dilute or inflate rewards. If governance is compromised or coerced, users can be rugged.
hypotheses.impact: Retroactive reward changes, inconsistent accounting, potential over- or under-payment.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_fromEpoch > block.number` (or at least `>= current epoch`) so rewards can only be set for future epochs.

hypotheses.title: VotingEscrow.withdraw does not reset delegated for delegatee
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` requires `locked_.delegatee == msg.sender` (i.e. the caller must be the delegatee, meaning the lock is undelegated). It then sets `newLocked.delegated -= amountToSend` and `newLocked.delegatee = address(0)`. However, if the user had previously delegated to someone else and then undelegated, the `delegated` amount may not match `amount`. More critically, the function does not update the delegatee's lock if the user had delegated to a different address — but the `require` prevents that. The real issue is that `newLocked.delegated` is set to 0 after the checkpoint, but the checkpoint uses `newLocked` with `delegated` already reduced, so the slope change is recorded correctly. However, if `locked_.delegated < amountToSend` (e.g. due to a previous partial delegation), the subtraction underflows and reverts, locking the user's funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user delegates part of their lock to a delegatee, then undelegates. The `delegated` amount is reduced by the undelegate logic, but `amount` remains the same. When the user calls `withdraw`, `newLocked.delegated -= amountToSend` underflows because `delegated < amount`, causing the transaction to revert and the user's funds to be permanently locked.
hypotheses.impact: User funds are frozen in the contract; they cannot withdraw their locked CANTO.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `newLocked.delegated = 0` instead of subtracting, or ensure `delegated` is always equal to `amount` when undelegated.
